all_of: one component generates a message with a strict library and a different component re-parses it with a lenient one
a value the attacker controls is written into a header AND into the body of the same generated message
the rendered sink takes parsed output without sanitising it
any_of: the generator is CPython older than 3.11.11 / 3.12.8, where email.policy.verify_generated_headers does not exist yet
the reading parser accepts 'Header : value' with whitespace before the colon
a template engine autoescapes the value, but the reading parser will honour a charset that re-introduces the escaped bytes

chain.action: read the front-end JavaScript and list every endpoint plus the exact sink
chain.why: the sink was shadow.innerHTML fed by a SECOND parse of the OpenSSL-verified bytes, not by the first parse, which decides where the payload must live

chain.action: pin the generator's language version from the Dockerfile before trusting any local test
chain.why: the header guard differs between CPython releases; testing on a newer local interpreter reports a false negative

chain.action: find a header form the generator emits but its own guard does not recognise, and confirm the reading parser accepts it
chain.why: 'Header : value' with a space before the colon passes re(r'\n[^ \t]+:') and is still honoured by mail-parser, overriding the genuine header

chain.action: use an RFC 2047 encoded-word to carry raw CRLF through the reading parser into a value the app echoes back
chain.why: it turns a single reflected field into full header and body injection on the NEXT generated message

chain.action: encode the payload in a charset the template engine has no opinion about
chain.why: UTF-7 spells '<' as '+ADw-', so autoescape is a no-op and the parser decodes it back to real tags

chain.action: recover the generator's PRNG when the structure depends on a random boundary
chain.why: each multipart boundary leaks one full 32-bit MT19937 output plus 31 bits of the next, so ~640 observed boundaries reconstruct the state exactly

chain.action: exfiltrate through the application's own API using the victim's stored token
chain.why: no outbound network is required and nothing external has to be hosted

first_confirming_probe.request: send one message whose Subject is 'x\nFrom : <other identity>', then read back what the application's own parser reports as the sender
first_confirming_probe.expected: the parser reports the injected identity, not the genuine From header the generator wrote
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: the generator rejects the newline, or the parser still reports the genuine sender, meaning the space-before-colon form is not honoured

blast_radius: read-only against the target's own data, but the bot endpoint is globally serialised behind a lock and each run costs ~15s; the collection phase writes several hundred messages into your own mailbox, so never point it at a shared account.
known_traps: the injected boundary delimiter is itself part of the message text, so email.generator._make_boundary() matches '^--<b>(--)?$', calls it a collision and re-rolls the boundary to '<b>.0' -- the prediction is right and the exploit still fails silently; a single trailing space on the delimiter line defeats the anchored regex and is still a legal RFC 2046 delimiter

the same attacker string is used for BOTH the Subject header and the template body, so every injected line must also survive the generator's header guard; keep a space before any colon and no colon before the first whitespace on a line
CPython normalises a lone CR to LF inside a header value, so a bare \r is not a way around the guard
verify the generator's version from the Dockerfile: a newer local CPython adds verify_generated_headers and rejects payloads the target accepts
the recovered PRNG state dies with the process, so collection, recovery and attack must run in one pass
a boundary that collided reads as '<digits>==.0' and will not match a strict '={15}\d{19}==' regex, which makes a signed message look unsigned in your own tooling

verification.evidence: the flag was read from the GET /api/emails response body on the live target, delivered there by the admin bot's own browser POSTing localStorage.flag to /api/send

reuse_when: one library generates a message or document and a different library re-parses it, especially across languages
a template engine autoescapes a value that a downstream parser will later decode under an attacker-chosen charset
a structure depends on a boundary or token drawn from a non-cryptographic PRNG whose outputs are observable
an admin bot replies to attacker-controlled mail and the reply address comes from a parsed header
